stories.title: Amaknak Bridge: houses built into the hillside
stories.subtitle: Stone walls, hearths and paths beneath the floor
stories.description: Follow dated floors, rebuilding and household work on the knoll beside the Amaknak Channel.

scenes.title: A west structure with its own hearth
scenes.body: An early charcoal sample came from the west feature of the Structure 7 cluster. The excavation found carefully fitted walls, a hearth and two channels under the floor. The east wall contained a chimney built with stone and sea mammal ribs. The original excavators grouped this feature with the main building. Later fieldwork found evidence of separate construction. Its older charcoal range helps distinguish the two deposits.
scenes.note: The viewing year lies inside the published range of Beta-184633.

scenes.title: A hearth and a covered pit
scenes.body: Structure 2 had a ring of upright stones, long hearth channels and a slab-covered storage pit. Its floor charcoal gives an early date among the excavated house contexts. Ash accumulated in the fill. Knecht and Davis considered whether it indicated an interruption in activity at the site. The deposits leave the length and extent of any interruption unresolved.
scenes.note: The viewing year lies inside the published floor-charcoal range.

scenes.title: Two dates in a house pit
scenes.body: Charcoal from the floor of Structure 5 and charcoal in the fill above it produced overlapping published ranges. Excavation placed these materials in different deposits and distinguished traces of the occupied floor from material that accumulated later. The order of deposits can stay visible even when dating uncertainty makes the samples overlap.
scenes.note: The viewing year represents the dated floor context.

scenes.title: Rebuilding beside Structure A
scenes.body: At Structure 7, a newer building was laid over a smaller hearth. Its north wall and the adjoining northwest feature pressed against the earlier Structure A. On its south, a replacement wall followed the line of one that had collapsed. What appears tightly clustered in the final excavation reflects repeated acts of building and repair.
scenes.note: The viewing year is within the main room’s charcoal range. The individual repairs are ordered by stratigraphy.

scenes.title: Evidence of seasons around the village
scenes.body: Ringed seal bones include recently weaned animals, evidence that hunters could reach seasonal ice in spring or early summer. Fish and seabird remains point to other seasons and other parts of the coast. Household deposits preserve a different part of the settlement from the walls and hearths that it took to build a sheltered home.
scenes.note: Representative year in the dated site evidence, with no date assigned to an individual hunt.

scenes.title: Cooking stones and material for needles
scenes.body: The round Structure 3 was under four metres across. Central supports held its roof, and some floor caches preserved likely materials for everyday work. Excavators found cooking stones and albatross long bones suitable for making needles. A hearth sample helps date an episode in the life of the house. The associated fill accumulated after use.
scenes.note: The viewing year lies within the published hearth-charcoal range.

stories.title: Iliuliuk and Unalaska: the village beside the harbor
stories.subtitle: An excavated longhouse and a charted waterfront
stories.description: Read the 1875 Coast Survey chart through the village’s buildings, trade and relationship to the water.

scenes.title: A longhouse at Reese Bay
scenes.body: On another bay west of Unalaska Bay, an excavated longhouse had a shared floor about thirty metres long, with side spaces. Glass beads found in its floor and fill date the excavated context to the early contact period. The house itself preserves evidence of a local building tradition and a shared space adapted by its residents.
scenes.note: Representative year in the early-contact time span.

scenes.title: The first Holy Ascension church
scenes.body: Local builders and Ioann Veniaminov constructed the first Holy Ascension church in a village that already stood beside the harbor. Mission work included writing and translation as well as worship. The church brought another building form and institution into a long-inhabited Unangan setting.
scenes.note: Documented construction year.

scenes.title: A new building on the church site
scenes.body: A second church replaced the first in 1858. The same place would later hold the standing Holy Ascension church. Timber from earlier phases was kept in the fabric of the new church, so the sequence can be read in both the historical records and the surviving building.
scenes.note: Documented rebuilding year.

scenes.title: Buildings follow the narrow shore
scenes.body: Surveyors recorded a church and small structures along the thin strip of ground at Iliuliuk. The steep hill behind the settlement and the sheltered water in front are visible in their chart. The distribution of the building symbols records a shore-oriented village. Their identities and exact footprints cannot be read from the marks alone.
scenes.note: The first of the two survey years printed on the chart.

scenes.title: Charting the waters between islands
scenes.body: Depth soundings and notes on tides made the waters of Iliuliuk navigable to readers of the Coast Survey chart. Dall’s field notebook records trade in fox, seal and sea otter skins between communities. Read together, the documents show the village shore as both an inhabited place and a stop for people coming from elsewhere.
scenes.note: The second survey year. The Coast Survey issued the chart in 1875.

scenes.title: Older timbers in the standing church
scenes.body: The standing Holy Ascension church was built between 1894 and 1896. Its cross-shaped plan, tower and chapels changed the form of the building at the old church site. Reused timber carried parts of the earlier churches into this phase, and the craftsmanship found inside reflects the labor of local builders.
scenes.note: The viewing year lies within the construction range.

stories.title: Chaluka and Nikolski: a village beside its ancient mound
stories.subtitle: Ananiuliak, a layered settlement and successive chapels
stories.description: Follow the evidence from toolmaking and house floors to the standing village church.

scenes.title: Blades and shelters on Ananiuliak
scenes.body: People produced stone blades near the coast on what is now Ananiuliak Island. Excavated depressions also preserve evidence of shelters. The island holds a distinct younger village where houses and storage pits were arranged above a bluff. The two sites mark separate episodes of residence across the bay from Nikolski.
scenes.note: The viewing year represents the dated early Core-and-Blade site. The younger village remains unplaced.

scenes.title: A house floor inside the mound
scenes.body: Layers at Chaluka preserve long use of reef and marine resources. One excavated house has a stone perimeter, a slab hearth and shallow pits under the floor. Concentrations of awls, needles and pebbles preserve some of the work in the interior. A sequence of floors and deposits gives a longer view than this one house can supply.
scenes.note: The year is within the village’s rounded range. The excavated house has no separate verified calendar interval here.

scenes.title: An early chapel in the village
scenes.body: John Kriukov directed construction of a chapel. It belonged to a community with a much longer history of residence around the bay. A later building survey names this predecessor and records its year, while the village history places it among households already engaged in fishing and maritime work.
scenes.note: The HABS survey dates construction to 1806.

scenes.title: Driftwood becomes a chapel
scenes.body: The chapel consecrated in 1828 was designed by Ivan Veniaminov and built from driftwood. Its materials connect religious buildings to the coastal supply of timber, familiar in a region with few stands of trees. The HABS history distinguishes this chapel from the later standing church.
scenes.note: The dated event is the chapel’s consecration.

scenes.title: New work on Umnak
scenes.body: A sheep ranch established in 1926 followed a fox-farming boom on Umnak. The Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association traces both ventures through local history. Their place in the village story shows how families added work on land to the better documented maritime economy.
scenes.note: The community history identifies 1926 as the ranch’s establishment year.

scenes.title: A square tower and a hipped nave
scenes.body: The standing St. Nicholas Church was erected in 1930. Its nave has a hipped roof, while the sanctuary and narthex are gabled. Sergei Sovoroff and the Krukoffs contributed interior carving. The construction date establishes one phase in the village’s built history, while the interior continued to change afterward.
scenes.note: The event dates construction of the standing church.

stories.title: Canadian Shield — camps, waterways and inland communities
stories.subtitle: Life along the interior lakes and rivers
stories.description: Follow ancient hearths, sturgeon fisheries and portage routes from inland Labrador to Great Slave Lake, then see how fur trading, treaty-making and hydroelectric development changed life through 1934.

scenes.title: A fire at the caribou crossing
scenes.body: At Shak Selma by inland Labrador’s Kamestastin Lake, people worked white quartz beside a small fire. A pit received fragments of quartz, grey chert and broken tools. Charcoal from the pit and adjacent fire gave the same radiocarbon measurement. Across the lake outlet, caribou crossed the water where hunters could watch them arrive. These traces bring one early episode of work into a country where people timed their activities to movements of animals, ice and water.
scenes.note: The selected viewing year falls within the larger published probability component. The separate older component is reported in the record.

scenes.title: A different pit and another fire
scenes.body: From a terrace above the valley, people could watch animals moving down toward the narrows. Excavators at Napeu Atik found a bowl-shaped pit with white quartz, a finished stone tool and small pieces of burnt bone. One of those pieces supplied an age. This place resembles Shak Selma in its use of quartz, yet the two pits have different shapes and separate dates. Each tells part of the changing history of the lake.
scenes.note: The lake marker is shared with other Kamestastin sites. It gives the setting without revealing the archaeological findspot.

scenes.title: Chert on the other side of the narrows
scenes.body: People at Mistanuk worked Ramah chert in large amounts. They left debris alongside bone that had burned hot enough for its mineral fraction to survive. Across the narrows, white quartz dominates some of the early deposits. The difference raises a practical question about how people acquired stone and chose where to work it. A few kilometres of shoreline can hold several distinct histories of the same centuries.
scenes.note: The viewing year is within the calibrated range for the selected sample from Area A.

scenes.title: Copper and bark become one tool
scenes.body: A barbed copper point at Renshaw near Thunder Bay still held part of its bark binding. Copper salts helped preserve plant fiber wrapped around the shaft. Scientists dated a small piece of that fiber to the fourth millennium BCE. Other copper tools at Renshaw held traces of wood or cordage. What survives on the metal shows how people combined materials with different properties to make a tool they could handle.
scenes.note: The viewing year sits within the published calibrated range for the bark binding on one point.

scenes.title: Small tools in the northern forest
scenes.body: At Black Lake, a survey found small stone tools that the excavator attributed to Pre-Dorset toolmakers. The lake lies near the winter range of barren-ground caribou. Some groups may have timed visits to the forest to take advantage of the herds. Several other traditions are represented at Black Lake across much longer periods, so this assemblage marks one chapter in the history of the lakeshore.
scenes.note: The proposed years are based on comparison with other regional assemblages. There is no direct local determination for these objects.

scenes.title: Fish and food shared beside the water
scenes.body: At the Long Rapids of the Rainy River, sturgeon drew people to a place of gathering and ceremony. The archaeological complex includes traces of dwellings and Laurel earth mounds. Northwest at Wanipigow Lake, pots and food remains give a view into the use of forest and aquatic resources. Wild rice and goosefoot survive in the archaeological record there. River communities could gather, move and return as food became available in different seasons.
scenes.note: The viewing year falls within broad pottery phase windows. Features and food remains have distinct histories.

scenes.title: Camps within the caribou’s winter range
scenes.body: Stone points found near Black Lake resemble late Taltheilei objects from farther north. Archaeologist Sheila Minni read these finds alongside Denésųłiné histories of caribou hunting. She proposed that families could spend time in the forest when caribou foraged in smaller groups. The larger movements of the herds made travel and returning to particular camp places an important part of how people lived here.
scenes.note: The viewing year represents the excavator’s tentative 1300–1500 CE comparison window.

scenes.title: A mission and a trading post at a river mouth
scenes.body: Where the Métabetchouane River enters Lac Saint-Jean, a French trade post and Jesuit mission opened in 1676. The establishment included a house and chapel. It sat where water routes joined and where Indigenous travellers already stopped. A stone chimney base and traces of a burnt wall remain visible in the archaeological record. The post was one phase of work and gathering at the river mouth.
scenes.note: 1676 dates the establishment of the mission and post.

scenes.title: The canoe route through Obadjiwan
scenes.body: Obadjiwan sits where the shores of Lake Timiskaming narrow. Anishinabe families had travelled and used this place for a long time by the time Montréal merchants set up a trading post in 1720. Goods could move through the narrows and between inland waterways. Archaeological remains of chimneys and foundations tell part of the history of this establishment. The trade post changed hands later while the narrows remained a route between places.
scenes.note: 1750 falls within the documented trading-post period. The point locates the public locality.

scenes.title: Rebuilding an inland depot
scenes.body: In 1826 the Hudson’s Bay Company rebuilt Norway House near the Nelson River after the older post burned. At the inland depot, people and goods could move between Lake Winnipeg, Hudson Bay and parts of the north and west. The Cree Nation’s history describes it as both a trade centre and a meeting place. Later warehouses and other buildings give some idea of the scale of work that went into keeping so many people and places supplied.
scenes.note: This viewing date concerns the later post near Jack River House.

scenes.title: Winter quarters on Great Slave Lake
scenes.body: George Back’s Arctic Land Expedition set up winter quarters on the East Arm of Great Slave Lake in 1833. Denésųłiné families had long hunted and lived in the surrounding country. Some stone fireplaces still survive at Fort Reliance from its building history. Researchers have compared these remains with fireplaces made and adapted by Dene craftspeople elsewhere. Moving through the northern interior required cooperation with people who already knew the lake and its seasonal conditions.
scenes.note: The scene dates the winter station. It does not assign each surviving fireplace to a specific building year.

scenes.title: A treaty at the Northwest Angle
scenes.body: Anishinaabe leaders and Crown commissioners made Treaty 3 at the Northwest Angle of Lake of the Woods in October 1873. The Grand Council preserves the Paypom account of the treaty promises. Down the Rainy River, Rainy River First Nations families homesteaded around a place where generations had gathered for sturgeon. Their cabins and farms show ways people continued to live near the rapids during a new set of negotiations over land and livelihoods.
scenes.note: 3 October 1873 is the signing date. The homesteading record covers a phase that begins with the Treaty 3 period.

scenes.title: Negotiations where the rivers meet
scenes.body: English River and Clear Lake leaders met the Treaty 10 commissioner at Sakitawak in August 1906. The meeting included requests for supplies and assistance for elders and for families in distress. It took place in a town known for fur trading and Métis commerce and family connections. Sakitawak was already a gathering place in a larger network of family settlements around the lake, and the treaty meeting marked one event among many in its history.
scenes.note: 28 August 1906 is the documented signing date for this meeting.

scenes.title: Trade pressures move a gathering place
scenes.body: The Naskapi Nation dates a move from Fort Chimo to Fort McKenzie to 1915. Families had to travel to the new inland post to get supplies as the company shifted where it did business. Winter camps and hunting grounds remained central to how people lived. Starting with the 1916 operating period, families stopped at Fort McKenzie for supplies and returned after winter to trade, share news and prepare for the next season.
scenes.note: The relocation and the post’s main opening are dated separately in the records.

scenes.title: Rising water changes the shape of home
scenes.body: At Lac Seul, the Ear Falls dam brought water over homes, gardens, graves and wild rice grounds. Families at Kejick Bay saw a connected shore become an island. Others moved to higher ground. The project took land used for fishing and harvesting without Lac Seul First Nation’s consent. By 1934 people could see the results in their routes and livelihoods. The effects continued well beyond the last year shown.
scenes.note: The point shows Kejick Bay. The map does not depict the extent of flooding or specific lost homes.
